svg.aria-label: Diagram: the structure of a Google Cloud IAM condition, the three policy types that accept one, the different attribute sets available in each, the opposite failure directions when an expression cannot be decided, and the two grants that cannot carry a condition at all
svg.title: IAM Conditions: one condition object, three condition languages
svg.text: One condition object. Three condition languages. The sameness is what misleads.
title + description + CEL expression — identical everywhere, and not portable between policy types.
Allow policy role binding
(and PAM entitlements)
resource.type / .name / .service
resource tags
request.time, access levels
API attributes
The widest vocabulary of the three.
Deny policy rule
denialCondition
resource tag functions ONLY
No resource.type. No request.time.
Undecidable → THE DENY APPLIES
Fails closed.
Principal Access Boundary
policy binding
principal attributes only
principal.type, principal identity
Enforced ONLY if it evaluates true
Undecidable → not enforced.
Two guardrails, opposite failure directions
An undecidable DENY denies. An undecidable BOUNDARY leaves the boundary switched off. Same word, same syntax.
Tags are the only shared vocabulary — so tags are the access model
Every other attribute family is confined to one policy type. Resource tags work in allow bindings AND deny rules.
So any distinction you want enforced from both directions must exist as a TAG — not a naming convention,
not a resource type. The tag taxonomy is a prerequisite for conditional access, not an afterthought.
The feature is unavailable on the two things most in need of it
No conditions on LEGACY BASIC ROLES — Owner, Editor, Viewer. (The second functional cost of the #32 rename.)
No conditions when granting to ALL USERS or ALL AUTHENTICATED USERS. Public is binary.
Coherent rather than perverse: a conditional Owner grant would make an unreviewable grant look reviewable.
And a condition still cannot narrow anything (#33)
Adding a conditional binding beside an unconditional one for the same role changes nothing — the union
still contains the unconditional term. A binding is only ever an addition.
To time-box access you must REPLACE the grant, not annotate it.
Budget: around 100 conditional role bindings per allow policy before the overall size limit bites.
Narrower than it looks: the access levels attribute is available only when you use IAP.
An expression is not a portable statement of intent — it is a sentence in whichever dialect the policy speaks.
